chunks.section: DisMUSE: An Efficient Distributed Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization Approach with Theoretical Convergence Guarantee
chunks.text: Zhen Qin Zhiyao Zhang Yingbin Liang Jia Liu Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Affiliation: The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA

In recent years, singular-spectrum-based optimizers have attracted increasing attention due to their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network gradients, thereby enabling geometry-aware optimization. However, most singular-spectrum-based (SSB) approaches remain centralized, limiting their use in distributed learning infrastructures that exploit massive parallelism. Distributed SSB optimization is still at an early stage, with open questions about convergence guarantees and communication efficiency. To fill this gap, we propose the Dis tributed M oment u m-based S pectral E stimator ( 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} ), an efficient distributed SSB optimization framework for both data-center and federated settings. Using Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum as the spectral update, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} integrates a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator and achieves an O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) convergence rate, where K K and T T denote the number of nodes and local iterations per node, respectively. This rate matches the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. Building on this variance-reduced framework, we study two extensions. First, our 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} method with finite Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations preserves the same convergence order under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative factor. Second, we develop a communication-efficient variant based on low-rank (LR) momentum transmission and quantify the error it introduces to the stationarity bound, characterizing the trade-off between accuracy and communication cost. Distributed learning has become a core paradigm for modern machine learning systems, spanning data-parallel training, federated learning, and edge learning scenarios where computation and data are spread across multiple nodes. In such settings, optimization algorithms must handle stochastic gradient noise, statistical heterogeneity, and communication constraints. While a large body of prior work studies these issues for conventional vector-based methods such as SGD [ 9 ] and Adam [ 21 ] , these methods treat parameters as flat vectors. Much less is understood when parameters and gradients are naturally matrix-valued, as in Transformers and convolutional networks. Recently, Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization (SSBO) methods, such as Muon [ 16 ] , Shampoo [ 13 ] , and SOAP [ 49 ] , have attracted growing attention for their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network updates. Among them, Muon has garnered the most interest due to its exceptional efficiency in large language model (LLM) training. Muon also has a relatively simple implementation: it orthogonalizes a matrix-valued momentum before applying the update, yielding geometry-aware descent directions [ 28 , 15 ] . Despite the promise of these SSBO methods, both their theory and implementation remain largely confined to centralized training in the literature, leaving open the question of how they should be designed and analyzed in distributed settings.

However, developing SSBO-based methods for distributed learning is highly non-trivial due to several technical challenges. First , the nonlinear spectral mapping does not commute with distributed aggregation. Averaging locally transformed spectral directions is generally not equivalent to applying the spectral map after aggregating the underlying momentum estimates, which can introduce systematic bias. Second , data heterogeneity and noisy gradient estimates further exacerbate this nonlinearity challenge. In distributed stochastic training, deviations in the momentum estimators are coupled with the nonlinear spectral mapping and can lead to directional errors, suggesting that the matrix-valued estimator should be carefully controlled before applying the spectral map. Third , practical Muon-style implementations typically replace exact orthogonalization with finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations. The resulting approximation error must therefore be explicitly accounted for in the convergence analysis. Fourth , synchronizing full matrix-valued momentum variables incurs substantial communication cost. This high communication cost motivates low-rank communication, whose additional approximation error must also be carefully controlled. In this work, we focus on Muon-type SSBO algorithmic framework and propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator ( 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} ) method, a unified framework for distributed SSBO. The key idea of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} is to build a variance-reduced distributed SSBO backbone as the foundation for practical Newton-Schulz orthogonalization and communication-efficient low-rank synchronization. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• A variance-reduced Distributed SSBO Backbone: We first develop 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} with exact orthogonalization and full communication of matrix-valued momentum. A STORM-style recursive estimator controls the stochastic deviation of the matrix-valued momentum before the nonlinear spectral transformation. Under the stated assumptions, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} achieves an O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) convergence rate for averaged stationarity, where K K and T T denote the number of nodes and local optimization iterations per node, respectively, matching the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. • 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} with Finite-step Newton-Schulz Orthogonalization: We replace the exact orthogonalization step with a finite number of Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations and show that the same O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) convergence order is preserved under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative approximation factor. • Communication-efficient Low-rank Implementation: We extend 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} to a low-rank communication-efficient implementation, where nodes can transmit low-rank momentum factors instead of full matrices. We quantify the additional error introduced by low-rank communication through an additive accumulated term accounting for both client and server spectral truncation.

In this section, we provide an overview on three closely related research areas to put our work into comparative perspectives. 1) Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization and Muon: Recent progress in large-scale neural network training has led to a class of optimization methods that explicitly exploit the matrix structure of model updates by manipulating their singular spectra, rather than applying element-wise preconditioning, such as Shampoo [ 13 ] , SOAP [ 49 ] , and Muon [ 16 ] . These methods have demonstrated strong empirical performance on a variety of deep learning tasks [ 2 , 5 , 16 , 28 , 36 , 41 , 51 , 52 ] . In the literature, these methods are sometimes loosely referred to as “matrix-aware optimization” or “geometric optimization.” However, “matrix-aware methods” may respect tensor structure without necessarily operating on spectral properties (e.g., Adafactor [ 42 ] ), while “geometric optimization” broadly covers manifold-based updates without isolating spectrum-level control [ 1 ] . To avoid confusion, in this paper, we use the Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization (SSBO) terminology for methods that directly manipulate the singular spectrum of matrix updates.

Among SSBO-based approaches, Muon has garnered increasing attention. Muon orthogonalizes a momentum matrix before applying the update, thereby aligning the descent direction with the spectral geometry of the matrix-valued gradient [ 7 ] . In practice, Muon typically avoids exact singular value decomposition (SVD) by using iterative approximations such as NS orthogonalization [ 16 ] . Recent work has studied the convergence properties, geometric interpretations, and optimization benefits of Muon and related spectral optimizers [ 2 , 10 , 15 , 20 , 23 , 25 , 26 , 30 , 31 , 35 , 40 , 43 , 44 ] . However, existing studies remain largely focused on centralized training, leaving distributed SSBO with practical NS orthogonalization less understood. 2) Variance Reduction and Communication-Efficient Distributed Learning: Distributed learning in data-center, federated, and decentralized settings must address the challenges of communication costs, stochastic noise, and data heterogeneity [ 17 , 32 , 33 , 38 , 45 ] . Communication efficiency is commonly addressed through local updates [ 32 , 45 ] and compression techniques such as quantization, sparsification, and low-rank approximation [ 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 14 , 39 , 46 , 48 , 50 ] , while momentum-based variance-reduction schemes address node drift and stochastic noise under heterogeneous data distributions [ 19 ] . Decentralized learning further relies on peer-to-peer communication, with methods based on model averaging, compressed communication, and Gradient Tracking [ 22 , 27 , 33 , 34 , 37 ] . However, these methods are developed for conventional vector-based optimization and do not explicitly account for nonlinear spectral transformations applied to matrix-valued momentum or gradient estimators.

3) Muon in Federated and Distributed Settings: Recent works have started to investigate Muon-style optimization in the FL setting. Existing studies have considered the theoretical benefits of Muon in FL, including communication complexity, robustness to heavy-tailed noise, and learning-rate choices [ 53 ] ; bias-corrected federated Muon with control variates and inexact NS iterations [ 47 ] ; and local-global alignment to mitigate client drift under heterogeneity [ 29 ] . For convenience, we refer to these baseline methods as FedMuon-FA [ 53 ] , FedMuon-SF [ 47 ] , and FedMuon-LRSF [ 29 ] , respectively. Compared to these federated Muon methods, our main goal is to build a variance-reduced distributed SSBO backbone . 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} controls the stochastic deviation of the matrix-valued momentum estimator before applying the nonlinear spectral mapping, and uses this backbone for a unified treatment of exact orthogonalization, finite-step NS approximation, and communication-efficient low-rank synchronization. Such variance-reduced mechanisms were not considered in the above FedMuon-type methods [ 29 , 47 , 53 ] .

chunks.section: 3.3 Key Challenges in Distributed SSBO-based Algorithmic Design
chunks.text: Although SSBO-based approaches have shown promise in centralized training, developing distributed SSBO-based algorithms presents several structural challenges that do not arise in their centralized counterparts. These challenges mainly arise from the nonlinear spectral mapping applied to matrix-valued gradient or momentum estimators, which interacts with data heterogeneity, stochastic noise, and communication constraints. In what follows, we discuss these issues in detail and use them to motivate the design of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} . Challenge 1) Non-Commutativity and Aggregation Bias: A first difficulty comes from the fact that the nonlinear spectral mapping does not commute with distributed aggregation. Let M t ( k ) M_{t}^{(k)} denote the local momentum estimator maintained by node k k at iteration t t . Then, we have: 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K Orth ⁡ ( M t ( k ) ) ≠ Orth ⁡ ( 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K M t ( k ) ) . \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{Orth}(M_{t}^{(k)})\neq\mathrm{Orth}\bigg(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}M_{t}^{(k)}\bigg). As a result, averaging locally orthogonalized momentum directions is not equivalent to the spectral direction of the averaged global momentum in the centralized setting. This differs fundamentally from vector-based distributed optimization, where commutativity holds due to the linear averaging operation. The resulting discrepancy can introduce systematic bias, especially when local objectives or stochastic gradients differ across nodes. The non-commutativity suggests a key design principle in 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} : the algorithm should synchronize and control the matrix-valued momentum estimators before averaging locally transformed spectral directions.

In conventional vector-based updates, E t E_{t} emerges in the update in an additive fashion. In SSBO, however, the corresponding update perturbation becomes Orth ⁡ ( M t det + E t ) − Orth ⁡ ( M t det ) , \Orth(M_{t}^{\mathrm{det}}+E_{t})-\Orth(M_{t}^{\mathrm{det}}), which is not a linear or additive function of E t E_{t} . As a result, even if 𝔼 ⁡ [ E t ] = 0 \mathbb{E}[E_{t}]=0 , one still has 𝔼 ⁡ [ Orth ⁡ ( M t ) ] ≠ Orth ⁡ ( M t det ) \mathbb{E}[\Orth(M_{t})]\neq\Orth(M_{t}^{\mathrm{det}}) . Thus, stochastic noise in the momentum estimator can lead to biased and directionally distorted spectral updates. This makes variance control important not only for efficiency, but also for obtaining robust spectral directions. 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} addresses this issue using a STORM-style recursive estimator [ 12 ] to reduce the stochastic deviation of the matrix-valued momentum before applying the spectral mapping.

chunks.text: Challenge 3) Orthogonalization Approximation Error: Our basic version of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} is based on exact orthogonalization. However, in practical Muon-style implementations, exact orthogonalization is typically approximated by a finite number of low-complexity Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations. Let X t , q X_{t,q} denote the result after q q NS iterations applied to M t M_{t} . Then the actual update direction X t , q X_{t,q} differs from Orth ⁡ ( M t ) \Orth(M_{t}) by the approximation error X t , q − Orth ⁡ ( M t ) X_{t,q}-\Orth(M_{t}) , which may not be negligible. Moreover, this approximation error resides within the nonlinear spectral transformation and may propagate across iterations. This motivates our NS extension, where we theoretically quantify the finite-step approximation error and show that 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} retains the same finite-time convergence order under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition. Challenge 4) Communication Constraints: Lastly, distributed SSBO must account for the communication cost of synchronizing matrix-valued momentum variables. For M ∈ ℝ m × n M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , full communication requires transmitting m ​ n mn scalars per synchronization, which can be prohibitive in federated and bandwidth-constrained settings. A natural approach is to exploit low-rank structure and transmit low-rank momentum approximations. However, low-rank factorization is itself nonlinear and can introduce additional bias through truncation and aggregation. This motivates our low-rank extension of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} , where the resulting approximation error is explicitly controlled.

We evaluate 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} on image classification tasks to examine its empirical performance and the practical effects of finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) orthogonalization and low-rank communication. Additional implementation details, hyperparameter settings, and ablation studies are provided in Appendix D .

1) Dataset and Setting. We evaluate 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} on CIFAR-10 [ 24 ] using a widened ResNet-20 with Group Normalization. We consider K = 5 K=5 fully participating nodes with an IID data partition and report results over three random seeds. Each node performs τ = 5 \tau=5 local updates per communication round with a batch size of 128. Detailed training settings are provided in Appendix D.1 . 2) Baselines. We compare 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} with FedAvg [ 32 ] , FedAvg-SGDM (FedAvg with momentum), FedMuon-FA [ 53 ] and FedMuon-SF [ 47 ] . We also compare four 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} variants: 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} -Full SVD with exact orthogonalization and full-rank communication, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 ​ - ​ 𝖭𝖲 \mathsf{DisMUSE\text{-}NS} with finite-step NS orthogonalization, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} -Low Rank SVD with low-rank momentum communication, and 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} -Hybrid, which combines low-rank communication with NS orthogonalization.

3) Results. Our results highlight three aspects of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} . First, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 ​ - ​ 𝖭𝖲 \mathsf{DisMUSE\text{-}NS} improves test accuracy from 86.95 % 86.95\% for FedMuon-FA to 89.92 % 89.92\% , supporting the benefit of the STORM-based gradient estimator under the same epoch budget (Table 2 ). Second, NS achieves comparable accuracy to SVD ( 89.92 % 89.92\% versus 89.69 % 89.69\% ) while reducing mean training time from 98.61 to 48.88 minutes, a 2.02 × 2.02\times speedup (Figure 1(a) and 1(b) ). Third, rank- 32 32 compression reduces the simulated communication payload by 40.5 % 40.5\% , from 385.39 to 229.34 GB. 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 ​ - ​ 𝖫𝖱 \mathsf{DisMUSE\text{-}LR} and 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} -Hybrid achieve test accuracies of 85.08 % 85.08\% and 85.03 % 85.03\% , respectively, illustrating the accuracy–communication trade-off (Figure 1(c) ). Finally, the median relative direction error (defined in Appendix D.1 ) drops substantially from q = 3 q=3 to q = 5 q=5 and changes little with further iterations, supporting q = 5 q=5 as a practical choice for the evaluated matrices (Figure 1(d) ). We evaluate 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} on the Tiny Shakespeare dataset [ 18 ] using a four-layer causal Transformer for character-level language modeling. We consider K = 5 K=5 fully participating nodes that independently sample from a shared training pool and synchronize every five local updates. Detailed model architecture and training settings are provided in Appendix D.2 . 2) Baselines. We compare three variants of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} (exact SVD orthogonalization with full-rank communication, finite-step NS orthogonalization, and low-rank communication) with the FedAvg and FedAdam (FedAvg with local Adam) baselines. 3) Results. As shown in Figure 2(a) , the NS variant achieves validation loss close to the exact-SVD variant, while the low-rank variant retains competitive performance under compressed communication. Figure 2(b) shows that NS substantially reduces the spectral direction computation time compared with exact-SVD. These results show that the practical NS and low-rank variants retain much of the empirical performance of exact full-rank 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} .

We proposed 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} , a distributed spectral optimization framework combining Muon-style orthogonalized momentum with recursive variance reduction. Under the stated assumptions, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} achieves an O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) stationarity rate, which finite-step NS orthogonalization preserves under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition. We also derived explicit error bounds for low-rank communication and its combination with NS, accounting for accumulated client and server truncation errors.
